title: Detect a cycle in a linked list (Floyd's slow/fast pointer).
shortTitle: Detect a Cycle in a Linked List — Floyd's Slow/Fast Pointer

s1_definition.profdef: Floyd's cycle detection, also called the tortoise and hare, determines whether a linked list contains a cycle. A slow pointer moves one node per step and a fast pointer moves two; if there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually laps the slow pointer and they meet, and if the fast pointer reaches null the list is acyclic. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India links transaction nodes, and a corrupted import could accidentally point a node back into the chain, forming an endless loop that would hang a traversal. Rajesh sends two fingers around the chain, one slow and one fast; if the chain loops, the fast finger keeps circling and eventually catches the slow one, proving there is a loop.
s1_definition.oneliner: Move slow by one and fast by two; if they ever meet there is a cycle, and if fast hits null there is none.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Floyd's cycle detection, also called the tortoise and hare, determines whether a linked list contains a cycle. A slow pointer moves one node per step and a fast pointer moves two; if there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually laps the slow pointer and they meet, and if the fast pointer reaches null the list is acyclic. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India links transaction nodes, and a corrupted import could accidentally point a node back into the chain, forming an endless loop that would hang a traversal. Rajesh sends two fingers around the chain, one slow and one fast; if the chain loops, the fast finger keeps circling and eventually catches the slow one, proving there is a loop.

**One line to remember:** Move slow by one and fast by two; if they ever meet there is a cycle, and if fast hits null there is none.

sections.s2_technical:
Start both `slow` and `fast` at the head. Loop while `fast != null && fast.next != null`, moving `slow = slow.next` and `fast = fast.next.next`. After each move, if `slow == fast` (same node reference) a cycle exists and you return true. If the loop exits because fast became null, the list ends, so there is no cycle and you return false.

A code snippet on a transaction list: `boolean hasCycle(Node head) { Node slow = head, fast = head; while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; if (slow == fast) return true; } return false; }`. The comparison is reference equality because we are detecting a structural loop, not comparing values.

Why are they guaranteed to meet if a cycle exists? Once both pointers are inside the loop, the fast pointer gains one node of ground on the slow pointer every step, so the gap between them shrinks by one each iteration until it becomes zero; they cannot jump past each other because the gap changes by exactly one. In an acyclic list the fast pointer simply walks off the end and the guard stops the loop.

A senior nuance is that this uses constant memory, unlike the alternative of storing visited nodes in a hash set which is also O(n) time but O(n) space. The reference comparison is essential; comparing node values could falsely report a cycle on a list with duplicate values. This detection is also the first half of finding the cycle's starting node, which builds directly on the meeting point.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India builds transaction chains from imported data, and a bad import can create a loop where a later node points back to an earlier one, which would cause any traversal to run forever. Before processing, the service must detect such a loop. This is exactly how Floyd's cycle detection works — slow and fast meet if and only if there is a loop.

Problem 2 — Memory is constrained in the import path, so the constant-space pointer method is preferred over a visited-set.

The code shows a `ChainIntegrityChecker` with `hasCycle`, a demo on a clean chain and a deliberately corrupted looping chain.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a clean chain T1 to T4, and a corrupted chain T1 to T4 where T4 points back to T2.

Step 1: For the clean chain, slow and fast start at T1. Slow moves to T2, fast jumps to T3. They are different. Fast at T3 has a next T4 but T4's next is null, so after the next move fast becomes null and the loop ends, returning false.

Step 2: For the corrupted chain, slow and fast start at T1. Slow moves to T2, fast jumps to T3. Different, continue.

Step 3: Slow moves to T3, fast jumps from T3 to T4 then to T4's next which is T2, so fast is at T2. Different, continue.

Step 4: Slow moves to T4, fast jumps from T2 to T3 then to T4, so fast is at T4. Now slow equals fast at T4, so a cycle is detected and the method returns true.

Step 5: The checker reports no cycle for the clean chain and a cycle for the corrupted one, each using only two pointers and no extra storage.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Clean chain has cycle? false
2026-10-26 21:00:03 WARNING Cycle detected in chain
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Corrupted chain has cycle? true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Clean: T1→T2→T3→T4→null
    │ slow/fast advance; fast hits null
    ▼
  false

  Corrupted: T1→T2→T3→T4→(back to T2)
    │ slow=T2 fast=T3
    │ slow=T3 fast=T2
    │ slow=T4 fast=T4  → meet
    ▼
  true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Floyd's cycle detection, the tortoise and hare, decides whether a linked list has a loop using two pointers and no extra memory. I start a slow pointer and a fast pointer at the head, advance the slow one by a single node and the fast one by two nodes each step, and check whether they ever point at the same node. If they meet there is a cycle, and if the fast pointer reaches the end of the list there is none.

The reason the meeting is guaranteed when a cycle exists is a clean argument I always give. Once both pointers are inside the loop, the fast pointer closes the gap to the slow pointer by exactly one node every step, so the distance between them shrinks by one each iteration until it reaches zero. Because the gap changes by exactly one, the fast pointer cannot leap over the slow pointer without landing on it, so a meeting is inevitable. In an acyclic list the fast pointer just walks off the end and the guard stops the loop.

Two details matter. The comparison is reference equality on the nodes, not value equality, because I am detecting a structural loop and a list with duplicate values would otherwise produce a false positive. And the approach uses constant memory, which is its advantage over the alternative of storing every visited node in a hash set, which costs linear extra space.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the chain integrity checker. Transaction chains were built from imported data, and a bad import could point a later node back to an earlier one, creating a loop that would make any traversal run forever, so before processing I detected such loops with the tortoise and hare. Because memory was constrained in the import path, the constant-space method was preferred over a visited set. Explaining the one-and-two stepping, the shrinking-gap argument, and the reference-equality and memory points shows the interviewer I understand why Floyd's algorithm is correct and efficient.
